tldr: ReFineR is a training-free offline registration method that uses differentiable point splatting to finely align single camera images and dense LiDAR point clouds, reducing errors from several or tens of pixels down to sub-pixel accuracy.
hero_caption: Comparison of registration results using geometric cues (normals) only. ReFineR (especially in a two-stage setup combined with MatchAnything) achieves high-precision alignment that closely matches the Ground Truth.
overview:
In autonomous driving and robotics, extrinsic calibration between cameras and LiDARs is an essential preprocessing step. However, no matter how carefully calibrated beforehand, dynamic factors during operation—such as vibrations, temporal desynchronization, rolling shutter effects, and SLAM drift—leave residual reprojection errors of around 7 to 10 pixels per frame. At moderate distances, an offset of 10 pixels causes geometric discrepancies of up to 40 cm, severely corrupting semantic label transfer onto LiDAR point clouds and texture mapping.

To solve this, the authors developed "ReFineR", an offline framework implementing an analysis-by-synthesis approach (rendering a 3D model into an image and optimizing the pose by comparing it with the real image) via differentiable point splatting. Point clouds are rendered using splatting with attributes such as surface normals or LiDAR intensity, and the Lie algebra parameters of the camera pose are directly optimized via gradient descent using a differentiable Gradient Orientation Measure (GOM). Furthermore, based on a first-order approximation analysis of the pinhole camera model, they devised an "automatic point cloud rescale factor" that is independent of scene scale, enabling optimization across both indoor and outdoor environments using identical hyperparameters.

For evaluation, they built a new benchmark curated with pixel-level calibrations across six heterogeneous datasets, including ETH3D, CARLA, and nuScenes. By adopting a two-stage approach—coarsely aligning with an existing feature matching method (MatchAnything) and then refining with ReFineR—the method successfully converges from large initial errors of up to 100 pixels, achieving remarkable sub-pixel (sub-1-pixel) alignment on high-precision datasets.
contributions: Proposal of ReFineR, a training-free fine registration method for single images and point clouds, based on point splatting that is end-to-end differentiable from point cloud to camera pose, optimized with the Gradient Orientation Measure (GOM).

Derivation of a theoretical automatic rescale method based on pinhole camera parallax characteristics, eliminating the need to tune hyperparameters such as learning rates across indoor and outdoor scene scales.

Construction and release of a high-precision benchmark curated across six heterogeneous data sources (real-world LiDAR, SLAM point clouds, RGB-D, and simulators) to overcome the lack of accurate pixel-level ground truth in existing benchmarks.

sections.heading: Why "a few pixels of error" can be critical for robots
sections.summary: While camera-to-LiDAR calibration is often considered a solved problem, real platforms still suffer from residual errors of several pixels per frame due to vibrations and desynchronization. This section highlights the severe impact on HD mapping and multimodal learning, presenting the goals and contributions of this work.
sections.details:
Camera-to-LiDAR calibration is often assumed to be fixed once calibrated. In real-world environments, however, subtle timing desynchronization between sensors, strong mechanical vibrations, camera rolling shutter, and SLAM drift cause relative poses to fluctuate frame by frame. In fact, a detailed inspection of the large-scale autonomous driving dataset nuScenes reveals that even with the official calibration parameters, average residual reprojection errors of 7 to 10 pixels remain.

While a few pixels might sound negligible, an offset of 10 pixels expands to a lateral geometric discrepancy of about 40 cm for objects tens of meters away. This is detrimental to semantic label transfer from images to LiDAR point clouds (automated labeling), HD map construction, and texture mapping, causing boundary mismatches that render the data unusable. Crucially, because these discrepancies fluctuate over time, a single global calibration cannot fix them; each image requires fine individual registration.

Recently, high-performance LiDAR-SLAM systems have made it possible to obtain highly accurate, dense 3D point clouds accumulated over past scans. The authors focused on the analysis-by-synthesis paradigm: "render a virtual image from the 3D point cloud and optimize the camera pose so that it matches the actual camera image." Integrating modern differentiable rendering, ReFineR formulates a pipeline that is fully differentiable from camera pose to loss function. Rather than real-time localization, its target is high-precision offline processing, such as HD mapping and automated dataset generation.

sections.heading: The limitations of explicit matching and implicit rendering
sections.summary: Image-to-point cloud registration broadly splits into explicit methods that directly find correspondences and implicit methods that optimize poses by comparing rendered images. This section reviews prior work, highlighting challenges like poor generalization of pre-trained models and non-differentiability.
sections.details:
### 2.1 Explicit registration
If 2D-3D correspondences are known, the 6-DoF camera pose can be solved analytically using Perspective-n-Point (PnP) algorithms and RANSAC. Consequently, numerous deep-learning-based methods directly match 2D and 3D features (e.g., CorrI2P, CoFiI2P, Diff2I2P) or predict pixel-wise 3D coordinates (Pointmaps, such as SANet). However, these learning-based methods are typically trained on single-frame LiDAR or RGB-D data, suffering from severe generalization drops when fed super-dense point clouds aggregated across multiple scans.

### 2.2 Implicit registration
Another approach is analysis-by-synthesis, which renders point clouds onto the 2D image plane from a rough initial pose and optimizes the pose by evaluating visual similarity against the real image. Early works (such as Taylor et al. or Guislain et al.) relied on the Gradient Orientation Measure (GOM), mutual information, or HOG features. Because renderers back then were non-differentiable, they had to depend on inefficient derivative-free optimization like the Nelder-Mead method.

### 2.3 & 2.4 Differentiable rendering and Gaussian Splatting
With the recent advent of NeRF and 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS), differentiable rendering—which backpropagates gradients from rendering outputs directly to camera poses—has advanced rapidly. While some works align novel images to 3DGS models (e.g., GS-SLAM), they typically require pre-training a high-quality 3DGS model from dozens of RGB images of the same scene and rely heavily on photometric losses. They cannot be directly applied to typical LiDAR point clouds that lack dense RGB appearance and only contain geometry or intensity.

sections.heading: Geometric foundations: the mathematics of pixel error and parallax
sections.summary: This section defines pixel reprojection error as a metric for registration difficulty and models how infinitesimal camera motions lead to pixel displacements using a first-order Lie algebra approximation.
sections.details:
When evaluating registration discrepancies, looking solely at metric translation error fails to reflect registration difficulty correctly across different scene scales (e.g., distant outdoor views vs. close-up indoor scenes). Therefore, the root mean square (RMS) of pixel reprojection error—the pixel shift on the image plane when 3D points are projected—is adopted as the primary evaluation metric.

For an infinitesimal perturbation $\delta\tau \in \mathfrak{se}(3)$ of camera extrinsics (3 rotational and 3 translational degrees of freedom), the displacement of projected points can be first-order approximated using the Jacobian matrix $J$. Crucially, pixel displacement caused by rotation depends solely on camera intrinsics and image coordinates, whereas displacement caused by translation is inversely proportional to point depth ($X_{iZ}$). Distant points barely move on the image plane when the camera translates, while nearby points move substantially—this is parallax. Mathematically modeling this parallax effect forms the foundation for the automatic rescaling proposed in the next section.

sections.heading: How ReFineR works: pose optimization via splatting and gradient alignment
sections.summary: ReFineR consists of a four-stage pipeline: automatic point cloud scale normalization, image generation via differentiable point splatting, cross-modal comparison via the Gradient Orientation Measure (GOM), and gradient descent over the Lie algebra.
sections.details:
ReFineR assumes a coarse initial pose is provided as a starting point (with errors of several to tens of pixels, typically from standard calibration or odometry). The framework comprises four steps:

### 4.1 Point cloud rescale estimation
Indoor and outdoor scenes have vastly different depth distributions. Because of parallax, using the same translation learning rate in gradient descent causes updates in wide outdoor scenes to be too small, leading to local minima. To address this, the authors analyzed the uncertainty matrix $S$ derived from the Jacobian (decomposed into rotational $S_r$ and translational $S_t$ parts). They compute a scale factor $\alpha$ analytically by equating their Hilbert-Schmidt norms, ensuring that one unit of rotation and one unit of translation contribute equally to pixel reprojection error. Consequently, camera poses can be optimized using identical, fixed learning rates without any per-scene hyperparameter tuning.

### 4.2 Synthesis
For each point in the normalized point cloud, a spherical Gaussian (point splat) is assigned with a radius proportional to the distance to its nearest neighbor. To prevent isolated points from bloating, their projected radius is clamped to a maximum of 4 pixels. The Gaussians store attributes such as surface normals (computed from local geometry) or LiDAR intensity, and are rapidly rasterized.

### 4.3 & 4.4 Analysis & Comparison
Images rendered from point clouds and real camera images have fundamentally different modalities (colors vs. normals or intensity). However, they share strong correlation at object edges, where gradient orientations align. Therefore, ReFineR employs the Gradient Orientation Measure (GOM) loss, which maximizes the cosine similarity between gradient vectors computed via differentiable Sobel filters. For raw point clouds (geometry only), the normal components $(p^{nx}, p^{ny}, p^{nz})$ are compared against real grayscale intensity $i^g$; when intensity or color is available, corresponding channels are directly compared using GOM.

### 4.5 Optimization
Because every step from rendering to GOM computation is differentiable, gradients of the loss with respect to camera pose $\tau \in \mathfrak{se}(3)$ can be computed. Using the PyTorch Adam optimizer, gradient descent is performed on the Lie algebra with a fixed learning rate ($2\times 10^{-4}$). The optimization terminates dynamically when convergence criteria are met, typically reaching fine alignment within 100 to 200 steps.

sections.heading: Experimental results: reaching sub-pixel precision from 100-pixel shifts
sections.summary: Evaluations were conducted across 6 heterogeneous datasets (164 images in total). ReFineR achieved high registration accuracy far exceeding existing baselines, both on raw geometry-only point clouds and on intensity-augmented point clouds.
sections.details:
### 5.1 Experimental setup
The evaluation used 164 images across 6 data sources: ETH3D (high-precision terrestrial laser), Tanks and Temples, nuScenes (automotive LiDAR), Livox, RGBDScenes (Kinect), and CARLA (simulator). Images were scaled to a height of 1024 pixels (480 pixels for RGBDScenes). Poses were initialized with perturbations averaging 10 pixels of error. Comparisons were made against MatchAnything (state-of-the-art multimodal feature matching), Koide et al. (mutual information), Yuan et al. (edge alignment), and GS-SLAM (photometric loss).

### 5.2 Registration with raw point clouds (geometry only)
In the most challenging setting using only surface normals (Table 1), standalone ReFineR achieved sub-pixel accuracy (<1 pixel) on 41% of ETH3D images (compared to 8% for MatchAnything). However, for larger initial errors or noisy clouds, MatchAnything showed higher robustness. Combining both into a two-stage approach (MatchAnything* + ReFineR)—coarse alignment followed by fine tuning—achieved sub-pixel accuracy on 58% of ETH3D images and <2 pixels on 68% of CARLA scenes, outperforming all baselines across all thresholds. Methods relying on photometric loss (GS-SLAM) or histogram matching (Koide et al.) diverged or yielded low accuracy due to weak correlation between normals and RGB.

### 5.3 Registration with intensity and colored point clouds
When LiDAR intensity or RGB colors from calibrated setup cameras were available (Table 2), road markings and textures could be leveraged, boosting performance across the board. The proposed two-stage method reached nearly 100% sub-pixel registration on ETH3D and achieved the lowest pixel errors across all other datasets.

### 5.4 Ablation study and robustness to large errors
Ablation experiments (Table 3) confirmed that removing automatic rescaling drastically degrades performance, particularly in large-scale outdoor scenes (CARLA), validating the theoretical design. Furthermore, in tests where initial perturbations were gradually increased from 0 up to 100 pixels (Table 4), MatchAnything alone saturated with residual errors, while adding ReFineR brought the median error back down to under 2 pixels even from a 100-pixel offset.

sections.heading: Challenges with floating noise, dynamic objects, and manual ground truth
sections.summary: This section discusses failure modes caused by floating points and dynamic objects in the point cloud, occlusion issues near walls, and the precision limits of manual annotation for ground truth.
sections.details:
The proposed method has several clear limitations:

- Dependence on point cloud quality: Floating outliers or dynamic objects (pedestrians, vehicles) present during capture can cause inconsistencies between the rendered and camera images, corrupting gradient calculations.
- Handling occlusions: As a common challenge in analysis-by-synthesis, when the camera is close to a wall or point density is low, points behind occluding surfaces may be rendered, causing spurious edges that mismatch the real image.
- Parallax in color attributes: RGB colors assigned to point clouds in RGB-D or terrestrial scanners originate from auxiliary cameras, meaning the assigned colors themselves may contain residual calibration errors.
- Precision limits of ground truth: The manual point-to-pixel annotations used to create ground truth inherently contain 2 to 3.5 pixels of reprojection error, making human annotation precision a bottleneck for evaluating true sub-pixel limits.

sections.heading: A robust, training-free solution for offline fine registration
sections.summary: ReFineR combines differentiable rendering with the Gradient Orientation Measure and features scale normalization across diverse scenes. It provides a powerful training-free tool for high-precision offline 3D data creation.
sections.details:
In this paper, the authors proposed ReFineR, a training-free differentiable framework based on analysis-by-synthesis to finely register single images with dense point clouds. By combining automatic scale normalization derived from pinhole parallax analysis with the GOM loss capturing edge geometry, the method generalizes across scenes without any per-scene parameter tuning.

When paired with a global feature matching method, it reliably converges to sub-pixel accuracy even from initial errors of tens of pixels. Rather than serving as a real-time SLAM frontend, ReFineR is expected to be a foundational tool for offline pipelines that demand absolute geometric precision, such as HD map creation for autonomous driving and automated annotation transfer from images to 3D point clouds.

sections.heading: Appendix: theoretical scale normalization and benchmark construction
sections.summary: This section covers the mathematical derivation of the scale factor $\alpha$ from pinhole camera Jacobians, the differentiable HOG implementation, and details on manual ground truth curation for nuScenes and Tanks and Temples.
sections.details:
### Analytical derivation of scale factor $\alpha$
To balance the impact of rotation and translation on reprojection error, a coordinate change $X = \alpha X'$ is introduced. By equating the Hilbert-Schmidt norms of the rotation uncertainty matrix $S_r$ and the scaled translation matrix $S'_t = \alpha^{-2} S_t$, $\alpha$ is derived in closed form as the fourth root of the ratio of squared eigenvalues: $\alpha = (\sum \lambda_{t,i}^2 / \sum \lambda_{r,i}^2)^{1/4}$. This automatically normalizes any point cloud to a scale suitable for optimization.

### Benchmark dataset construction
Existing datasets like nuScenes and Tanks and Temples already exhibit several to tens of pixels of reprojection error under their official calibration parameters. For this benchmark, the authors manually selected about 15 prominent 2D-3D correspondences per image and minimized reprojection errors via Gauss-Newton optimization, curating high-precision ground truth with residual errors of 3 to 5 pixels on nuScenes and about 2 pixels on Tanks and Temples.

takeaways: Even "calibrated" standard datasets (such as nuScenes) contain 7 to 10 pixels of per-frame residual error, making individual refinement essential for high-precision tasks.
Because parallax causes rotation and translation to contribute differently to pixel displacement, analytically deriving a scale factor from Jacobian norms is highly effective for scale normalization.
When comparing different modalities between images and point clouds, the Gradient Orientation Measure (GOM)—which focuses on edge alignment rather than photometric values—is remarkably effective.

The recommended best practice is a two-stage pipeline: use a global matching method (like MatchAnything) for coarse pull-in, followed by differentiable-rendering-based local optimization (ReFineR) to reach sub-pixel precision.
limitations: Floating noise, dynamic objects, and occluded points rendered into the image can cause gradient mismatch and lead to local minima.

Requiring tens of iterative rendering and backpropagation steps per image, optimization takes tens of seconds, making it unsuitable for real-time online pose estimation (targeted at offline workflows).
Ground truth created via manual correspondence annotation has an accuracy floor of around 2 pixels, making it difficult to benchmark the method's true sub-pixel limits strictly.
